jina.title: A new genus of xenophyophores (Foraminifera) from Japan Trench: morphological description, molecular phylogeny and elemental analysis
jina.snippet:
Abstract

The deep-sea floor is inhabited by a number of unusual and enigmatic taxa, unknown in shallow waters. These include the xenophyophores, a group of giant protists that construct fragile agglutinated tests. Here, we describe Shinkaiya lindsayigen. et sp. nov., a new xenophyophore collected by the submersible Shinkai 6500 at a depth of 5435 m near the Japan Trench. The phylogenetic analysis performed on its complete small-subunit ribosomal DNA (SSU rDNA) sequence confirms that Sh. lindsayisp. nov. is a foraminiferan that is closely related to another xenophyophore, Syringammina corbicula Richardson, 2001, and to a monothalamous (single-chambered) foraminiferan Rhizammina algaeformis Brady, 1879. In terms of morphology, the new genus resembles Syringammina, but its test wall is thicker, softer, and more weakly cemented. Moreover, the SSU rDNA sequences of the two genera are highly divergent. Mass spectra analyses reveal unusually high concentrations of some elements, such as lead, uranium, and mercury. The granellare system (the cytoplasm and the organic sheath that encloses it) is apparently devoid of barite crystals, which are usually abundant as intracellular inclusions in xenophyophores, but is rich in mercury (with 12 times the concentration of mercury found in the surrounding sediment). Fecal pellets retained within a tubular system (stercomare) concentrate heavy metals, including lead and uranium (respectively, two and six times more than that of the sediment). Based on a comparison of the compositions of the agglutinated test wall, the granellare, the stercomare, and the surrounding sediment, we discuss the impact of xenophyophores on their habitat.

Located parallel to the east coast of the Japanese mainland of Honshu, is the Japan Trench (Fig. 1A). It extends 611 km and covers an area of 37,854 km² beyond 6000 m depth. The Japan Trench is formed as the Pacific Plate subducts beneath the Okhotsk (minor) plate at a convergence rate of approximately 9 cm/yr (Nishikawa et al. 2023). The deepest point is 8001 m at 36.0872° N, 142.7272° E (this study). In the north, a subducting seamount partitions it from the Kuril-Kamchatka Trench and, in the south, the westernmost seamount of the Joban Seamount Chain separates it from the Izu-Ogasawara Trench (Yamazaki and Okamura 1989). The Japan Trench is seismically active and known for tsunamigenic megathrust earthquakes (Ueda et al. 2023) that result in large mass wasting events at depth, resulting in large volumes of re-suspended sediments (Itou et al. 2000, Oguri et al. 2013, Kioka et al. 2019).

The deepest point is 7339 m at the south-western end of an elongated depression at 24.4752° N, 127.4088° E (this study).

Occultammina is a genus of xenophyophorean foraminifera known from the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. It is notable for being the first known infaunal xenophyophore as well as for being a possible identity for the enigmatic trace fossil Paleodictyon .

Distribution and habitat

[ edit ]
Like all other known xenophyophores, Occultammina is found in the deep ocean; the first known specimen was first discovered in 1980 at a depth of 8,260 m (27,100 ft) in the Ogasawara Trench , off the coast of Japan and described in 1982 by a joint research team from the University of Copenhagen and the University of Tokyo . Occultammina is infaunal; it typically is found at a depth of 6 cm (2.4 in) or less below the sediment's surface. [ 2 ] It was the first known infaunal xenophyophore. [ 4 ]

A xenophyophore found just below the surface of a box core of modern deep-sea sediment from the Japan Trench has a threadlike plasma body that extends through horizontal, anastomosing networks of organically bound sediment tubes (the organism's test). seltz.title: In 2014, a camera rig sank for over an hour into the western Pacific, far from any island, and still hadn't reached the bottom. At that depth, sunlight had vanished thousands of meters above, the water sat barely above freezing, and the pressure was over a thousand times what you feel at sea level.
seltz.snippet:
In 2014, a research ship sat alone in the western Pacific, hundreds of kilometers from the nearest island. No land in any direction, no other vessels, just open water. Under the hull, a camera rig was sinking, falling for more than an hour, and it still hadn’t touched bottom. At that depth, sunlight was a rumor, a thing that had given out thousands of meters above.

The water sat barely above freezing, and the pressure squeezing the rig from every side was more than a thousand times what a person feels at sea level. Nobody on that ship expected to see anything alive. This was supposed to be the most lifeless place on the planet. They were wrong.

When the footage came back, something was moving in it—something that, by everything scientists believed at the time, had no business being where it was filmed. That one clip launched more than a decade of expeditions into the most hostile place on Earth, a trench so deep that if you dropped Mount Everest into it, the summit would still sit about two kilometers underwater. What has been pulled out of that darkness since is stranger than most horror films: a fish held together by the pressure crushing it, a shrimp wearing metal armor, a single cell the size of a mango, and entire communities of animals that have never once needed the sun. We spend billions aiming telescopes at distant planets, hoping for any trace of alien life.

Meanwhile, there is an alien world at the bottom of our own ocean, and we’ve barely switched the lights on. The trench curves through the western Pacific, east of Guam, like a fingernail scratch across the sea floor. It runs about 2,000 kilometers end to end, roughly the distance from London to Moscow.

***Occultammina*** is a genus of xenophyophorean foraminifera known from the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. It is notable for being the first known infaunal xenophyophore as well as for being a possible identity for the enigmatic trace fossil *Paleodictyon*.

## Distribution and habitat

Like all other known xenophyophores, *Occultammina* is found in the deep ocean; the first known specimen was first discovered in 1980 at a depth of 8,260 m (27,100 ft) in the Ogasawara Trench, off the coast of Japan and described in 1982 by a joint research team from the University of Copenhagen and the University of Tokyo. Further specimens referred to *Occultammina* sp. have been found at a depth of 4,844 m (15,892 ft) in the Porcupine Abyssal Plain, in the North Atlantic. Further studies have expanded its geographical and bathymetric range from 3,000 and 8,260 metres (9,840 and 27,100 ft) in the Ogasawara Trench and from 4,500 to 4,800 metres (14,800 to 15,700 ft) in the North Atlantic, and also recorded its presence at 6,440 m (21,130 ft) in the Japan trench. *Occultammina* sp. has also been recovered at a depth of about 4,050 metres (13,290 ft) near the Clipperton fracture zone, off the coast of western Mexico.

*Occultammina* is infaunal; it typically is found at a depth of 6 cm (2.4 in) or less below the sediment's surface. It was the first known infaunal xenophyophore.

*Occultammina* is found at turbidite facies in today's oceans.

seltz.title: On May 10, 2014, the robot Nereus was working nearly 10 kilometers down in the Kermadec Trench, northeast of New Zealand, when its ship lost contact after seven hours of a nine-hour dive. Pieces later floated to the surface.
seltz.snippet:
On the tenth of May 2014, the remotely operated vehicle Nereus was working on the floor of the Kermadec Trench, northeast of New Zealand, at a depth of nearly ten kilometers. It had been built specifically for places like this. Five years earlier, it had reached the deepest point on Earth and returned safely. Seven hours into a nine-hour dive, the ship above lost contact with it.

Later, pieces of Nereus were seen floating on the surface. Now compare that with something else. In 2022, a camera lowered into a trench south of Japan filmed a fish. A small, pale fish drifting toward a bait bag at a depth of more than eight kilometers.

No pressure hole, no rupture. Just soft tissue doing what fish normally do. And deeper than both of those, at 10,898 meters in the Mariana Trench, a camera recorded a plastic bag. A machine destroyed.

A fish in its element. A shopping bag at the bottom of the world. Those three facts lead to a single question: what actually lives at the bottom of the ocean, and did we get there before we ever saw it? In the Caribbean Sea, south of the Cayman Islands, the seafloor is slowly spreading apart.

Researchers following a chemical trace along that rift found black smokers pumping fluid hotter than 400 degrees Celsius at a depth of 4,960 meters. The water cannot boil only because the weight of the ocean above prevents it. They named the field Piccard after the naturalist William Beebe, the first scientist to watch deep-sea animals alive in their own habitat. The vent column rises more than a kilometer through the water.

Its chimneys are crowded with a species of shrimp that was new to science. Even today, this is the deepest hydrothermal vent system ever discovered. Below it, no black smoker has ever been confirmed. Keep

## How deep is the Mariana Trench?

The Mariana Trench reaches 10,935 meters (35,876 feet) at its deepest point, called the Challenger Deep. This is deeper than Mount Everest is tall, if you could place Everest at the bottom of Challenger Deep, its peak would still be 2 kilometers underwater.

---

## The Deepest Place on Earth

Nearly 11 kilometers below the Pacific Ocean surface, at a point called Challenger Deep, the water exerts pressure over 1,000 times greater than the air at sea level. No sunlight reaches these depths. The temperature hovers just above freezing.

And yet, the Mariana Trench is inhabited. Not by sharks or giant squid, not by megalodons or sea monsters, but by creatures so unusual they seem to belong to a different planet entirely. Understanding what lives at the bottom of the ocean is one of biology's great ongoing discoveries, and most of it has been made in the last twenty years.

## How Deep Is the Mariana Trench?

The Mariana Trench is 2,550 kilometers (1,585 miles) long, running along the floor of the western Pacific east of the Mariana Islands. Its deepest point, called Challenger Deep, reaches 10,935 meters (35,876 feet).

To visualize this:

- Mount Everest is 8,849 meters tall. Place Everest at the bottom of Challenger Deep and its peak would still be 2 kilometers underwater.
- The temperature at the bottom is 1 to 4 °C (34 to 39 °F).
- Water pressure at the bottom: 1,086 bars (15,750 PSI). This is over 1,000 times atmospheric pressure at sea level.

Semipsammina fixa Tendal, 1975, the type species of

the new species.

Tendal et al. (1982) speculated that ‘infaunal xenophy-
ophores with very regular polygonal networks of sedi-
ment tubes may exist.....and these could be makers of
the well-known trace fossil Paleodictyon’. Swinbanks
(1982) illustrated several small tubular fragments of
a xenophyophore from the Japan Trench (6640 m) in
which the tubes did indeed form polygons. According
to Swinbanks (1982), most of his fragments ‘have
characteristics of the family Syringammindae’; he did
not identify them further but speculated on their pos-
sible relationship to Paleodictyon.

ultimate.title: Faunal biodiversity of the lower abyssal and hadal zones of the Japan, Ryukyu and Izu-Ogasawara trenches (NW Pacific Ocean; 4534-9775 m)
ultimate.snippet:
Located parallel to the east coast of the Japanese mainland of Honshu, is the Japan Trench (Fig. 1A). It extends 611 km and covers an area of 37,854 km² beyond 6000 m depth. The Japan Trench is formed as the Pacific Plate subducts beneath the Okhotsk (minor) plate at a convergence rate of approximately 9 cm/yr (Nishikawa et al. 2023). The deepest point is 8001 m at 36.0872° N, 142.7272° E (this study). In the north, a subducting seamount partitions it from the Kuril-Kamchatka Trench and, in the south, the westernmost seamount of the Joban Seamount Chain separates it from the Izu-Ogasawara Trench (Yamazaki and Okamura 1989). The Japan Trench is seismically active and known for tsunamigenic megathrust earthquakes (Ueda et al. 2023) that result in large mass wasting events at depth, resulting in large volumes of re-suspended sediments (Itou et al. 2000, Oguri et al. 2013, Kioka et al. 2019).

The deepest point is 7339 m at the south-western end of an elongated depression at 24.4752° N, 127.4088° E (this study).

The organisms from the Izu-Ogasawara Trench, particularly near the Boso triple junction (Fig. 10C), can tentatively be classified as xenophyophores, exhibiting morphological features similar to known species such as __Shinkaiya lindsayi__ (described from Japan Trench specimens at approximately 5435 m depth, Lecroq et al. (2009)) or __Syringammina__ spp. (pers. comm. Andrew Gooday, NOCS, UK). These organisms also resemble presumed xenophyophores documented in seafloor imagery from the NE Atlantic at around 3000 m depth, as discussed by Tendal and Gooday (1981). The branched forms, especially those depicted in Fig. 10B, display complex, irregular reticulated structures akin to those observed in the Japan Trench, but are not always clearly associated with physical structures (Fig. 10D).

# A new genus of xenophyophores (Foraminifera) from Japan Trench: morphological description, molecular phylogeny and elemental analysis
...
The deep-sea floor is inhabited by a number of unusual and enigmatic taxa, unknown in shallow waters. These include the xenophyophores, a group of giant protists that construct fragile agglutinated tests. Here, we describe Shinkaiya lindsayigen. et sp. nov., a new xenophyophore collected by the submersible Shinkai 6500 at a depth of 5435 m near the Japan Trench. The phylogenetic analysis performed on its complete small-subunit ribosomal DNA (SSU rDNA) sequence confirms that Sh. lindsayisp. nov. is a foraminiferan that is closely related to another xenophyophore, Syringammina corbicula Richardson, 2001, and to a monothalamous (single-chambered) foraminiferan Rhizammina algaeformis Brady, 1879. In terms of morphology, the new genus resembles Syringammina, but its test wall is thicker, softer, and more weakly cemented. Moreover, the SSU rDNA sequences of the two genera are highly divergent. Mass spectra analyses reveal unusually high concentrations of some elements, such as lead, uranium, and mercury. The granellare system (the cytoplasm and the organic sheath that encloses it) is apparently devoid of barite crystals, which are usually abundant as intracellular inclusions in xenophyophores, but is rich in mercury (with 12 times the concentration of mercury found in the surrounding sediment). Fecal pellets retained within a tubular system (stercomare) concentrate heavy metals, including lead and uranium (respectively, two and six times more than that of the sediment). Based on a comparison of the compositions of the agglutinated test wall, the granellare, the stercomare, and the surrounding sediment, we discuss the impact of xenophyophores on their habitat.
